title: How to program an arm day (the Natural Hypertrophy example)
summary: How to program an arm day, using his own two arm days as examples. An arm day opens with one heavy arm movement in a giant set that hits every target muscle, then narrows toward isolation of priority muscles. It avoids full-range-of-motion compounds and sits between taxing lower body days. Its goal is a pump and active recovery, not fatigue. He adds forearm, shoulder and upper back work and never curls below 3-4 reps.

claims.claim: An arm day focuses only on the arms but isn't only isolation work; it contains no heavy full-range-of-motion compound lifts, gives the body rest, and the pump helps recovery, so it is useful even if you don't train for size.
He opens every training day with a heavy movement; on arm day, being biceps-obsessed, he starts with heavy dumbbell cheat curls or very strict EZ-bar curls.
If you prioritize triceps, open the arm day with a triceps-focused heavy press instead: close-grip bench, slingshot bench, pin press or board press.
Place the arm day between two CNS-taxing heavy days such as a squat day and a deadlift day, or on one of your rest days; it won't take away from strength or CNS recovery.
You don't need to camp at the cable machine on arm day; dumbbell movements work fine.

Add forearm, shoulder and upper back work to arm day: the arm pump helps recruit more muscle, and resilient muscles like the upper back can handle a lot of volume while forearms rarely get direct work.
Most of his biceps and forearm work happens on arm days, while much of his triceps work happens on bench days.
His first arm day opens with a 4-round giant set: heavy dumbbell cheat curls 3-7 reps, front raises 6-10, behind-the-head dumbbell extensions 6-12, barbell wrist curls 6-10, Dorian rows 6-12.
The opening giant set of an arm day should hit every muscle group you plan to target, warming up the whole body and setting the theme of the workout.
His second giant set uses lighter weight: strict curls, skull crushers (triceps long head) and wide-grip chin-ups, repeated four times.
Structure an arm day wide to narrow: start with many muscle groups, then as sets go on work fewer muscles with more isolation, ending on the ones you care about most.
On his first arm day he prioritizes the triceps long head over the lateral head.

His first arm day continues with Arnold curls, dumbbell bench flyes, two-arm behind-the-head dumbbell extensions and wide-grip chin-ups for his small lats, then close-grip preacher curls, finger curls and pullovers.
His arm day lasts about three hours and he has done arm days for at least five years; beginners should start much shorter because they lack the stamina.
His second arm day opens with heavy EZ-bar curls, heavy side delt raises, dumbbell extensions, wide neutral-grip pull-ups for the lats, and snatch-grip Pendlay rows for the upper back.
His two arm days share almost no exercises but train exactly the same muscles; to emphasize triceps, swap curls for a bench accessory or extensions.
His second arm day continues with overhead pin presses for triceps and delts, barbell wrist curls and heavy seated preacher curls.
An arm day means moving very heavy weight through a very specific range of motion to isolate the arms.
Avoid full-range compound lifts like the bench press or overhead press on arm day: they train the arms but are too tiring.
You should finish an arm day energized and pumped, not tired; tiredness is expected after heavy squats or deadlifts, but training relatively small arm muscles shouldn't wear you out.
Heavy movements for the rest of the body can go on arm day (rows, close-grip bench, weighted chin-ups, pin presses) if you use a harder variation that needs less weight or a reduced range of motion.
Exact sets and reps matter less than exercise selection; adapt them to what works for you, since they are just volume and intensity manipulation.
Never do 1-rep maxes on curls; he never goes below 3-4 reps, and when he does 3 it is because he could have done 4.
Arms are less resilient than the rest of the body: train them hard but don't overreach.
